explain.say: Your throat is a crossroads: air goes to the windpipe and food goes to the gullet. Swallowing is a quick routine that sends food the right way.

explain.say: You start it by choice: the tongue pushes the chewed food back. After that the reflex takes over, and the soft palate at the back of the roof of your mouth lifts to seal off your nose.

explain.say: The voice box rises and a flap called the epiglottis folds down over the windpipe like a trapdoor, while the vocal cords close and breathing pauses for a moment.

explain.say: The food slides into the gullet, the oesophagus. Rings of muscle squeeze in waves behind it, called peristalsis, pushing it down to the stomach in a few seconds, even if you are upside down.

faq.a: The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap of cartilage at the top of the voice box. When you swallow it tips down to cover the windpipe, so food and drink go into the gullet instead of the lungs.
asks: Tell me about the epiglottis flipping down
What stops food going into the lungs?

faq.q: Why does food sometimes go down the wrong way?
faq.a: If you talk, laugh or breathe in while swallowing, the windpipe may not be fully closed and a bit of food or drink slips in. Sensors detect it and you cough to clear it out.
asks: What does going down the wrong way mean?

faq.a: Peristalsis is a wave of muscle squeezing that moves along a tube. In the gullet, the muscle behind the food tightens while the muscle in front relaxes, pushing the food down to the stomach.
asks: Tell me about the gullet squeezing
How does food get to your stomach?

faq.a: Yes. Because the gullet pushes food along with muscle waves, gravity is not needed. Astronauts swallow normally in space.
asks: Does gravity pull food to your stomach?

faq.q: Why can't you breathe and swallow at the same time?
faq.a: Air and food share the throat. During a swallow the airway is sealed off for about a second, so breathing pauses automatically.
asks: Why do we stop breathing when we swallow?

facts: Swallowing starts voluntarily but its throat and gullet stages are automatic reflexes.
Food takes roughly 5 to 10 seconds to travel down the oesophagus to the stomach.
Peristalsis lets people swallow even when upside down or in weightlessness.
